text.p: Europe's golfers will not be revisiting the "greens from hell" next year.
Ken Schofield, the tour's executive director, confirmed on Thursday the British Masters will move from Collingtree Park in Northampton to a venue yet to be named.
Fury developed among stars such as Colin Montgomerie and Seve Ballesteros in August when Collingtree staged the first qualifying event for next September's Ryder Cup.
The greens were so badly hit by a disease known as meadow grass decline, all the players were said to be close to walking out as scores soared into the 80s.

Announcing the 1997 schedule, Schofield said: "The disintegration of the greens there fractured the confidence of the players and the administration. What we have set out to do since is rebuild confidence. We have a very big job to do."

No total prize-money figures for next year have been given yet but the circuit is expected to break the 30 million pounds ($48.8 million) barrier compared with around 23 million ($37.4 million) in 1996 and six million ($9.8 million) 10 years ago.

At Collingtree, Ryder Cup captain Ballesteros called for changes in the way the tour is run and two weeks later he, Montgomerie and Nick Faldo were among 50 players who met in Paris to air their grievances and discuss the way forward.
Tour deputy executive director George O'Grady said on Thursday: "The tour is the players and we intend to communicate with them more."

The 1997 tour starts with two weeks in Australia, then possibly three in South Africa before coming north of the equator for Dubai and the Moroccan Open and finally reaching Europe at the Portuguese Open from March 13-16.
The final Ryder Cup qualifying event is on August 28-31 at the BMW International in Germany.
